cues.text: A Woman Healed and Transformed
Mary Magdalene takes her name from Magdala, a fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.
The Gospel of Luke introduces her among women who accompanied Jesus and the Twelve, supporting them out of their own resources.

This reveals her material means and deep personal gratitude, since Luke tells us plainly that Jesus had cast out of her seven demons, a severe affliction from which she had evidently been dramatically and completely delivered.
From the moment of that healing forward, Mary appears consistently among Jesus's most devoted followers.
She was not one of the Twelve, but part of a wider circle of women disciples.
The Gospels take care to record their faithful presence, even when the male disciples' own courage occasionally faltered.
A Circle of Women Who Never Left
Luke names Mary Magdalene alongside Joanna, wife of Herod's steward Chuza, and Susanna, among "many others" who provided for Jesus and the Twelve out of their own resources.
This detail is easy to pass over quickly, but reveals a genuine community of women disciples supporting Christ's public ministry financially and practically from very early on.
The Gospels take pains to record this partnership, even though the culture of the day rarely gave women's contributions such deliberate attention.
Present When Others Fled
The Gospels place Mary Magdalene among the women who witnessed the Crucifixion.
John's Gospel specifically depicts her standing near the cross during the Crucifixion.
She stood alongside the Mother of Jesus and the beloved disciple , while most male followers, by their own later admission, had scattered in fear for their own safety.
This same faithful presence carried her, along with several other women, to Jesus's tomb early on the third day, bringing spices to properly anoint a body.
Jewish burial custom, interrupted by the onset of the Sabbath, had not yet allowed them time to prepare.
This act of simple, grieving devotion would place her, by God's providence, at the very center of the most important event in human history.
The First Witness of the Resurrection
Finding the tomb empty and the stone rolled away, Mary Magdalene, according to John's Gospel, remained weeping outside.
This continued even after the other women and disciples had gone, until a figure she first mistook for the gardener spoke her name — Mary .
In that single spoken word, she recognized the voice of the Risen Christ himself.
Jesus's instruction to her was direct and unmistakable: go to my brothers and say to them, I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God .
This commissioned one faithful, grieving woman, before any of the Apostles had yet encountered the risen Lord, to be the very first herald of the Resurrection.
"Apostle to the Apostles"

Mary Magdalene's obedience to this commission—running to tell Peter and the other disciples, I have seen the Lord —earned her the title Apostola Apostolorum , "Apostle to the Apostles," from ancient times.
This designation was used already by early Church writers and later given renewed emphasis by St. Thomas Aquinas .

It recognized that the first person entrusted to proclaim the central message of the entire Christian faith was not one of the Twelve, but this faithful woman who had simply refused to leave the tomb.
A Reputation Long Misunderstood
For many centuries in the Western Church, Mary Magdalene was popularly conflated with the unnamed sinful woman who anoints Jesus's feet in Luke's Gospel.
She was also conflated with Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus —an identification modern biblical scholarship has largely set aside.
The Gospel texts themselves do not clearly support treating these as the same woman.
Whatever the truth of these separate identifications, the genuine, textually secure Mary Magdalene of the Gospels needs no borrowed story.
Her greatness is established as a woman healed by Christ, faithful at the cross when others fled, and the first witness of his rising.
Legacy
In 2016, recognizing the singular dignity of her witness, Pope Francis elevated Mary Magdalene's liturgical celebration to the rank of a Feast.
This gave her liturgical celebration the rank of a Feast, the rank commonly assigned to celebrations of the Apostles.
The Congregation for Divine Worship explicitly framed the decree as an invitation to reflect more deeply on the dignity of women and on the greatness of the mystery of divine mercy.
She remains a permanent, luminous reminder that the Gospel entrusts its central proclamation not only to the mighty or officially credentialed.
It entrusts that proclamation to whoever, healed by Christ's own mercy, remains faithful enough to stand at the foot of the cross and at the door of the empty tomb.
